t: Redirect police budget increase to youth employment and establish community budget standards
rt: MOTION, dated 06/22/2020, submitted by Councilmembers Sittenfeld, Young, Kearney, Seelbach and Landsman; WE MOVE that the increase to the Cincinnati Police Department's existing Fiscal Year 2020 Budget in the City Manager and Mayor's Fiscal Year 2021 Budget be redirected to youth employment and opportunities. WE FURTHER MOVE that this can be achieved by modestly adjusting the projected attrition for Fiscal Year 2021, and by a 1.5 - month delay in the next recruit class. WE FURTER MOVE that as Cincinnati's economy bounces back from the recession caused by COVID0-19, and, in turn, City revenue also grows, that a standard be established and adopted for how each new dollar is allocated as pertains to the ratio of funding for the Cincinnati Police Department versus funding for Human Services, such as housing, health, youth services and employment, social services, violence prevention, and Black and Brown Business support. This forward-looking policy guideline should be created through significant community conversation and engagement with the goal of a more balanced, holistic budget that is proactive rather than reactive in its investment in people.

t: Statement supporting Freeman District as transformative Black community investment
rt: STATEMENT, dated 02/20/2020, submitted by Councilmember Dennard, The economic wealth gap that persists between the Black and White communities in the City of Cincinnati is staggering. There is a clear history of redlining in our city that has led to and continues to perpetuate a racial wealth gap today. Black communities continue to be under-resourced and under-valued. There needs to be focus and intentionality with development that attracts and retains Black people all the while building Black wealth. The Freeman District is a major step in that direction. It is a transformative investment lead by the Black community and Black business owners. It's a version of Black-owned entertainment, dinning and living right in the heart of our city. Our rhetoric regarding inclusion and diversity in the City of Cincinnati must be followed up with action.
sm: Councilmember statement supporting Freeman District development to address racial wealth gap and build Black community wealth.

t: COVID-19 public participation protocols for City Council meetings
rt: STATEMENT, (EMERGENCY ORDER) (Public Participation Protocols) submitted by Mayor John Cranley, Pursuant to Article III of the Cincinnati Charter, Article XVIII of the Administrative Code of the City of Cincinnati, recent orders from the Ohio Department of Health, and in anticipation of large crowds at City Hall during the finale weeks before summer recess, it is hereby ordered that the City Administration shall establish and enforce protocols protective of the public health during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic for public participation and comment during any City Council or Council committee meeting. The reason for the protocols is the need to allow reasonable forum for citizens' comments while ensuring the safety and health of all participants and City staff at such meetings. Such protocols shall establish that social distancing requirements will be enforced in Council Chambers and any other impacted spaces within City Hall and that any person offering public comments shall be required to exit City Hall after speaking in chambers for so long as there are individuals queued to offer public comment in order to safely accommodate members of the public. The aim of this order is to ensure that all persons seeking to speak in-person at Council Chambers have an opportunity to do so. The public comment protocols shall provide appropriate space for members of the media as well as any other health or safety protocols determined by the City Administration to be necessary. In order to safely accommodate public participation, the Clerk of Council shall also provided opportunities for remote participation and comment. The Clerk of Council shall work with the City Administration to ensure all protocols are enforced. This order has the force of law and is an emergency measure issued pursuant to Article III of the Cincinnati Charter, Article XVIII of the Administrative Code of the City of Cincinnati and recent orders from the Ohio Department of Health. This Order is based upon the existence of a condition of public danger or emergency, as established by the Mayor's Declaration of Emergency in relation to the COVID-19 pandemic and shall continue in effect in accordance with its term.
sm: Establishes COVID-19 safety protocols for public participation at City Council meetings during the pandemic.

t: COVID-19 Emergency Declaration Amendment for Safe City Reopening
rt: STATEMENT, (DECLARATION OF EMERGENCY) submitted by Mayor John Cranley, The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic presents emergency conditions and dangers to the public health and welfare without precedent in the past 100 years.  After declaring a state of emergency and instituting severe measures to "flatten the curve," the State of Ohio has begun to reopen Ohio's economy, sector by sector, concluding that initial steps toward reopening can be safely taken in accordance with good hygiene and social distancing measures. Consistent wit the State's reopening efforts and at the request of the City Manager, I hereby amend, revise and tailor the existing COVID-19 declaration of emergency to this new phase of the response to the pandemic, pursuant to Article III of the Cincinnati Charter and Article XVIII of the Administrative Code of the City of Cincinnati. The emergency condition and danger that forms the basis for this amended and revised declaration is the ongoing public health emergency caused by the pandemic and the need to enable the safe reopening of the City including, but not limited to, reopening of retail businesses, restaurants and workplaces in the City. By this revised declaration, the Mayor retains emergency authority to issue orders under the limited circumstances necessary for the safe reopening of Cincinnati. This declaration is consistent with the statewide health emergency declared by Governor DeWine, the issuance of Ohio Department of Health's compulsory health orders and related guidelines and the fundamental need to protect vulnerable populations during this pandemic. This Order supersedes the March 11, 2020, emergency declaration as to any conflicts and hereby amends any such conflicts consistent with the provisions of this declaration. All emergency orders issued under the March 11, 2020, declaration are hereby terminated except for the Outdoor Street Dining and Social Distancing  order dated May 12, 2020, a copy of which is attached to this declaration, which is extended. If extended, emergency orders shall continue in effect in accordance with the terms of Article XVIII of the Administrative Code. This amended and revised declaration shall be issued to the news media for the widest possible dissemination to the citizens of Cincinnati. This declaration shall be effective June 29, 2020.
sm: Amends COVID-19 emergency declaration to enable safe reopening of Cincinnati businesses and workplaces during pandemic recovery.

t: Update Council Rules to Record Silence as Yea Vote on Voice Votes
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Landsman, WE MOVE that Council Rules be updated by adding the following:Council Rule 6.4a - Voice Vote. For purposes of a voice vote, when a member is present and entitled to vote, a member's silence will be recorded as a yea vote. A voice is any vote where a year or nay roll call vote is not required, such as on a motion or a suspension of readings of legislation. At the Presiding Officer's discretion, the vote may be announced. Pursuant to the City Charter, a roll call vote is required for an emergency clause and passage of legislation.

t: Declaration of Emergency for COVID-19 Public Health Threat
rt: STATEMENT, submitted by Mayor Cranley, upon consultation with and at the request of the City Manager, and based upon the emergency or public danger currently existing in the City of Cincinnati, I hereby issue this declaration of emergency pursuant to Article III of the Cincinnati Charter and Article XVIII of the Administrative Code of the City of Cincinnati. The emergency or public danger arises from verified reports of positive cases of contagion from COVID-19, an infectious disease caused by the novel coronavirus, in Ohio, Kentucky and Indiana and based on the recent declaration of a state-wide emergency in Ohio issued by Governor DeWine in relation to that public health emergency. The declaration of emergency is necessary to allow the City of Cincinnati to take appropriate action to protect against the spread of COVID-19 in Cincinnati and to protect vulnerable populations in Cincinnati and the Greater Cincinnati region from contracting COVID-19. Information received by the City Administration has established that the number of positive cases of COVID-19 may be significantly underreported due to the lack of adequate medical testing materials made available by the federal government, adding to the scope of the potential public health threat and potential need or rapid action. The public danger or emergency declared herein shall commence at 3 p.m. on the 11th day of March 2020, and shall terminate only upon the undersigned officer's determination that such emergency conditions no longer exist, or pursuant to the provisions of Article XVIII of the Administrative Code. The duration of such declared emergency shall not extend beyond two weeks from the date and time of the declaration unless extended by action of City Council. The declaration shall be issued to the news media for the widest possible dissemination to the citizens of Cincinnati.
sm: Mayor declares citywide emergency effective March 11, 2020 to protect against COVID-19 spread and enable rapid response actions.

t: Permanent debarment for contractors convicted of fraud or misrepresentation
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Dennard, I MOVE that the City of Cincinnati permanently debar any person, company or organization from doing business with the city if they are convinced of misrepresentations and/or fraud in order to secure contracts with local, state or federal government for which they wouldn't ordinarily qualify. Said person, company and/or organization cannot do work for the City of Cincinnati as a contractor or subcontractor. Further, said person, company or organization cannot be on payroll, listed as a principal, owner or executive nor serve on the Board of Directors for any entity seeking to do business with the City of Cincinnati. Further, I direct the City of Cincinnati to review and edit sections of the Municipal Code that would allow the City to suspend a person or business from receiving City contracts or participating in City procurements where they are charged with a crime that if they are convicted would be a basis for their being debarred. This option would be in addition to the provisions of Section 321-153 (see attached) that provide for debarment. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Permanently bars contractors convicted of fraud from doing business with the city and reviews related Municipal Code sections.

t: Adopt new equity-focused evaluation criteria for Human Services Advisory Committee funding decisions
rt: MOTION, dated 03/18/2020, submitted by Councilmember Seelbach, WE MOVE that the City Council adopt new evaluation criteria for the Human Services Advisory Committee to use during its Evaluation process prior to the recommendation of Human Services Funding aware recommendations. The new evaluation criteria should address: 1) Whether the use of city funds by the human services provider is equitable to the diversity of the city's demographics, recognizing that minority communities are underserved through traditional means and may have less options for service, thereby reaffirming their need for support within the Human Services Fund; 2) How the provider ensures outreach into and impact within the city's African American community and other traditionally underserved communities; 3) That HSAC should consider the outcomes of equitable engagement and successful impact as a key factor during the evaluation process, giving emphasis to organizations whose data and track records show success at greater impacts into traditionally underserved and minority communities.
sm: Establishes new evaluation criteria emphasizing equity and outreach to underserved communities for human services funding recommendations.

t: CUF Neighborhood Parking Proposal Review and Implementation Plan
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Landsman, WE MOVE that the City Administration review the recommended neighborhood parking proposal as presented by CUF community leaders in May of 2020 and provide a plan to fully fund and implement the following recommendations by December of 2020: Encourage better utilization of existing off-street parking in the Calhoun/McMillan Business District: - Public garages: expand availability of monthly passes, provide better signage and wayfinding, evaluate pricing and adjust accordingly, and assist with marketing garages to the groups that previously used on-street unmetered parking such as UC commuters and employees of businesses. Discourage free long-term parking in the currently unmetered on-street spaces in the residential areas to the south and west of UC: - Provide signage and enforcement for street sweeping, therefore requiring cars to be moved at least monthly or else they are progressively warned, then ticketed, then ultimately towed should they not comply. Work with UC to promote medium term parking (ex: satellite lots) in less congested areas to move commuter cars off of residential streets. Promote and fund non-single occupancy vehicle transportation options to UC students and faculty, and provide easier options for long, medium and short distance commuters: - Encourage and assist in providing infrastructure for bikes, scooters, and ride share programs such as Uber and Lyft. - Assist in advancing an Uptown circulator shuttle in cooperation with SORTA and UC. - Create One Way Streets with Bike Lanes: Flora, Victor, Stratford, Chickasaw, Rohs, Wheeler, Moerlein, &Ohio. WE MOVE that after these changes above have fully implemented (December of 2020), the City Administration, working alongside neighborhood leaders, will then assess the need for a residential parking permit program. Assuming there is still a need for greater intervention, the neighborhood leaders and City Administration will than provide a plan to fully fund and implement a residential parking permit program unique to the CUF community by June of 2021 (end of FY21). (SEE STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Directs administration to review and implement CUF community parking recommendations by December 2020.

t: Mayor declares COVID-19 state of emergency for Cincinnati
rt: STATEMENT, submitted by Mayor Cranley, pursuant to Article III of the Charter and Article XVIII of the Administrative Code of the City of Cincinnati, I declared a state of emergency earlier today based on the critical need to allow the City of Cincinnati to take appropriate action to protect against the spread of COVID19 in Cincinnati and to protect vulnerable populations in Cincinnati and the Greater Cincinnati region from contracting COVID19. During the period of emergency, I will work closely with the members of City Council. City Manager Patrick Duhaney, the City Administration, and the City of Cincinnati Board of Health to ensure that appropriate communication is taking place within all levels of City government and that appropriate notifications are being distributed to those in the Greater Cincinnati region, through the City of Cincinnati website, media sources and other appropriate channels. City Manager Patrick Duhaney will continue to carry out his role as the City's chief administrative and chief executive officer in order that City operations can proceed efficiently and with minimal disruption and to ensure that appropriate administrative actions are being carried out to minimize the public health risks associated with COVID19.
sm: Mayor declares emergency to protect Cincinnati from COVID-19 spread and coordinate city response efforts.

t: Track liquor license issuance by race and gender to monitor potential inequities
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Dennard, I MOVE that the City of Cincinnati track the issuance of liquor licenses within the City boundaries by race and gender. I further move that we create a requirement for the application process to list race and gender effective immediately. I direct the City of Cincinnati take an inventory of existing liquor license to better understand the current landscape of valid and current liquor license so that we can monitor any potential inequities in our process. This information will need to be taken, tracked and monitored by City Administration and reported to City Council. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)

t: Principled and Collaborative Path Forward for CPS and City Council Agreement
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Pastor, (A Principled and Collaborative Path Forward for CPS and City Council) In order to solve this problem, WE MOVE the following as a principled and collaborative path forward: 1. Temporarily re-adopt the 1999 Agreement. a. The expiration of the re-adoption shall be when City Council and the School Board execute an agreement based off the neutral third-party or July 31, 2020, whichever comes first. 2. Hire a mutually agreed upon 3rd party. 3. City Council and School Board agree to work constructively to implement the recommendation of the neutral third-party. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Proposes temporarily re-adopting 1999 CPS agreement and hiring neutral third-party to resolve disputes.

t: Study police bias findings and issue recommendations for addressing disparities
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Pastor, Whereas reporters from the nonprofit newsroom Eye on Ohio, The Cincinnati Enquirer and researchers from Stanford University's Big Local News program examined police stops to assess how the three largest Communities in Ohio use public safety resources and to identify potential bias in policing; and, Whereas, the report found police in Cincinnati made 120% more total stops per resident in predominantly black areas; therefore, WE MOVE that the City Administration study the findings of the report and issue recommendations that address: 1. Chief Issac's statement: "We need to look at the reasons why in predominately African American communities there (is) more police contact," and 2. The findings of the report that found once pulled over, African Americans made up 75% of all Cincinnati stop arrests. 3. The understaffing of the Citizen Complaint authority and the cost associated fully funding it.
sm: Directs administration to study police bias report findings and recommend solutions for disparities in stops and arrests.

t: Create Veterans Ride Free Program with SORTA for 3 Years

sm: Directs administration to work with SORTA to establish free transit program for veterans lasting at least 3 years.

t: Study cost of fertility, surrogacy and adoption coverage for city employees
rt: MOTION (AMENDED), submitted by Councilmember Pastor, In order to fully pro-family and pro-worker, it is the responsibility of the Cincinnati City Council to do our best to implement policies that mirror best practices. All families deserve the opportunity to create and raise a family. To be a competitive city, we must adopt competitive policies. WE MOVE that the City Administration determine the cost of providing fertility, surrogacy and adoption coverage as part of the City's preferred provider option plan and its benefits offerings for city employees.
sm: Requests administration to determine cost of adding fertility, surrogacy and adoption benefits for city employees.

t: Motion requiring independent audit before approving CPS Tax Incentive Agreement
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Pastor, Seelbach, Dennard, Young, Murray and Mann, The growth of the City of Cincinnati and the success of Cincinnati Public Schools are directly related to each other. In order to support our city and our public school students, Cincinnati City Council must engage in the necessary due diligence to determine what is best for both our city's growth and our city's schools. WE MOVE that City Council and the City Administration take no action regarding the Tax Incentive Agreement with the Board of Education of the City School District of the City of Cincinnati without first receiving the report of an independent audit by a neutral third party to calculate the hold harmless number. The "hold harmless" number is the amount necessary to hod CPS harmless based on all relevant factors.
sm: Requires independent audit to calculate hold harmless amount before approving Tax Incentive Agreement with Cincinnati Public Schools.

t: Transfer Bond Hill-Roselawn capital improvement funds to CEAI for community revitalization
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Dennard I MOVE that the City of Cincinnati transfer the balance of the capital improvement project account no. 980x164x171637, "Bond Hill-Roselawn Community Partnership", specifically the amount that is not currently encumbered for a development project in accordance with the existing developer agreement, so that such remaining funds can be reallocated and made available for use by the Community Economic Advancement Initiative ("CEAI") solely for the purpose of providing resources for capital improvement in the Bond Hill-Roselawn community for the purpose of stabilization and revitalization. The original agreement as outlined in Ordinance No. 175-2016 (see attached) created a partnership between CEAI, the Port of Greater Cincinnati Development Authority ("the Port") and the City of Cincinnati. Availability of such funds will be contingent upon an amendment of the original development agreement between CEAI, the Port and the City of Cincinnati, for which funds were originally appropriated in the amount of $3,000,000. Upon execution of the amended development agreement between those parties, Council requests that the Administration provide an ordinance carrying out the terms described in this motion for Council consideration. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Transfers remaining capital improvement funds to CEAI for Bond Hill-Roselawn community stabilization and revitalization projects.

t: Require public disclosure of Area Median Income data for affordable housing

t: Study design alternatives to prevent misuse of center turn lanes as passing lanes
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Jeffreys and Cramerding, WE MOVE, that the Administration report back to Council within ninety (90) days on the cost and feasibility of design alternatives that prevent drivers from using a shared, bi-directional, center turn lane as a passing lane. t: Update City Charter provisions on ballot initiatives for transparency and timeframes
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Keating, WE MOVE for the Law Department to begin drafting an ordinance updating the City Charter with provisions on ballot initiatives to allow for more public transparency and longer timeframes for the Law Department to prepare ballot initiatives for a Council vote. WE FURTHER MOVE the Law Department makes the appropriate changes to the Charter to require a petitioner to file final ballot measure language with the Clerk of Council prior to collecting any signatures. This should follow the mold set by the City of Columbus: a clear title to the ordinance along with a singular subject matter. This should be paired with fixing the ambiguous language within the City Charter regarding candidate petitions and their affidavits. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Motion to draft ordinance updating City Charter ballot initiative provisions for transparency and clearer processes.

t: Report on Financial Implications of Cincinnati Southern Railway Sale to Norfolk Southern
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Cramerding and Harris, WE MOVE that the administration prepare a report within the next thirty (30) days on the financial implications of the sale of the Cincinnati Southern Railway to Norfolk Southern, pending approval from Cincinnati voters. The report should address the possible spending opportunities for these funds, including the extent to which these funds can be used to remedy the City’s outstanding $500 million of critical failing infrastructure, the City’s operating budget, and the City’s pension liability. It should consider these challenges to our city budget as well as others that impede attaining a structurally balanced budget. It should also address how the spending of these funds is restricted and what they cannot be used for. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Requests administration report on spending opportunities and restrictions for potential Cincinnati Southern Railway sale proceeds.

t: Charter Amendment for 0.3% Income Tax Increase to Fund Affordable Housing
rt: ORDINANCE (EMERGENCY), submitted by Emily Smart Woerner, City Solicitor, TO SUBMIT to the electors of the City of Cincinnati an amendment to the Charter of the City which would require the City of Cincinnati to raise income and withholding taxes by three-tenths of one percent (0.3%), if subsequently approved by the electorate, annually beginning January1, 2025, which new taxes shall be deposited into a non-lapsing special revenue fund restricted only to finance housing affordable to households with income up to 80 percent of the area median income as established by federal law with 65 percent of the fund restricted to support housing affordable only to households with incomes up to 30 percent of the area median income; which new taxes shall fund such housing throughout the city of Cincinnati through grants, subsidies, and loans, including to third party housing developers, which may be of low or no interest, and/or forgivable; which new taxes can be spent to increase, preserve, maintain, repair, improve, and pay off indebtedness, related to privately owned homes and rental properties owned and rented by people with incomes up to 80 percent of the area median income as established by federal law; which new taxes can be spent to provide down payment assistance, mortgages, loans, financial counseling, and construction loans to people with incomes up to 80 percent of the area median income; and which up to five percent of annual revenues collected from the new tax may be used to support city staff and operations established for the purposes of administering the funds; and which imposes long-term restrictive covenants on property that receives funds from these taxes to maintain affordability and provide first right of refusal to purchase rental property funded through these taxes to tenants and the City, and shall be administered in consultation with an 11 member board of private citizens.
sm: Submits charter amendment to voters for 0.3% income tax increase dedicated to affordable housing fund.

DETERMINING that the goals of the Task Force are to recommend necessary improvements to the Mayor and City Council that will transform Court Street, between Vine and Walnut Streets, into a vibrant and pedestrian-oriented civic space that can provide flexibility for programming and encourage strong indoor/outdoor spaces for adjacent businesses, and at the Task Force's own discretion, to expand the study area to include Court Street from Elm Street to Main Street, to examine a range of design, infrastructure, technical, and program improvements to achieve both the vision and goals approved by City Council, and to make specific recommendations for methods by which to accomplish the transformation of Vine Street south of Central Parkway into a vibrant, safe commercial, retail and residential corridor by converting Vine Street south of Central Parkway to a two-way street, and the transformation of both Eighth and Ninth streets into vibrant, safe, commercial, retail, and residential corridors by converting each, in section or in whole, into two-way streets; and DETERMINING that among sources of funds for such proposed improvements will be Tax Increment Financing (TIF) funds from the Downtown/OTR West Equivalent Fund; AUTHORIZING the City Manager to take all appropriate steps to ensure that the Departments of Transportation and Engineering, Community and Economic Development, and City Planning shall provide all necessary support to the Task Force; ACCEPTING and appropriating the generous financial support from 3CDC in an amount up to $25,000, in order for the City to retain urban design and transportation consultants needed by the Task Force to complete its work and generate necessary studies and analysis; ACKNOWLEDGING that the Task Force will be able to make recommendations regarding the use of a matching amount of funds of up to $25,000 from the City of Cincinnati to be used for the purpose of funding eligible capital expenses arising from the Task Force's study recommendations; t: Report on establishing Community Investment Trust program for resident building ownership
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, WE MOVE for a report within sixty (60) days on establishing a Community Investment Trust (CIT) program in Cincinnati, including feasibility, costs, and steps for implementation. Portland, Oregon established its CIT program in 2015. The mission of the CIT “Learn-Invest-Profit” program is to move investors from “owing to owning.” Residents of the building and of the surrounding communities, especially low to moderate income residents, are encouraged to be investors. Each investor invests a small dollar amount ($10-$100) every month into the building in which they are living. As time passes, the investors buy more shares in the building as the building value appreciates and the loan amount decreases. The investors pay expenses for the property. They receive an annual dividend when there is a profit. There is also a provision, a Letter of Credit, to protect the investors from losses. Investors may cash out at any time. Being an investor requires residency in the building or the surrounding community (as defined by zip codes), and participation in financial literacy classes. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Requests report on creating program allowing residents to invest in and eventually own their buildings.

t: Report on establishing Community Investment Trust program for resident building ownership
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney and Councilmember Johnson, WE MOVE for a report within sixty (60) days on establishing a Community Investment Trust (CIT) program in Cincinnati, including feasibility, costs, and steps for implementation. Portland, Oregon established its CIT program in 2015. The mission of the CIT “Learn-Invest-Profit” program is to move investors from “owing to owning.” Residents of the building and of the surrounding communities, especially low to moderate income residents, are encouraged to be investors. Each investor invests a small dollar amount ($10-$100) every month into the building in which they are living. As time passes, the investors buy more shares in the building as the building value appreciates and the loan amount decreases. The investors pay expenses for the property. They receive an annual dividend when there is a profit. There is also a provision, a Letter of Credit, to protect the investors from losses. Investors may cash out at any time. Being an investor requires residency in the building or the surrounding community (as defined by zip codes), and participation in financial literacy classes. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Requests report on creating program allowing residents to invest in and eventually own their buildings.

t: Develop comprehensive litter prevention and removal plan with performance analysis
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Cramerding and Jeffreys, WE MOVE that the administration utilize the Office of Performance and Data Analytics and, if necessary, outside consultants to identify best practices, compare peer cities, and develop a plan for comprehensive and proactive litter prevention and removal plan, and to inform council of the cost of such a plan. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration produce a report within ninety (90) days which identifies and outlines short-term improvements. This report shall include potential resources that may re allocated for implementation of improvements identified along with budget update recommendations. t: Create parking enforcement blitzes in high impact areas
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Harris, Johnson, Walsh, Jeffreys and Cramerding, WE MOVE that the administration create and execute a plan for parking “blitzes’ where resources are dedicated towards ticketing and informing offenders in high impact areas. This should focus on issues related to quality of life, including blocking the sidewalk or other public right-of-way, fire hydrants, bus stops or lanes, accessible ramps or other accessible infrastructure, bike lanes, fire lanes, and street cleaning dates. This should be accompanied by periodic updates on the effectiveness of the blitzes. (BALANCE ON FILE IN THE CLERK’S OFFICE) (STATEMENT ATTACHED).
sm: Administration directed to create parking enforcement blitzes targeting quality of life violations in high impact areas.

t: Study automatic dismissal of old low-level misdemeanor warrants for economic relief
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney and Councilmember Johnson, Individuals who already are struggling financially can be further harmed by old, low-level misdemeanor crimes that can prevent them from obtaining employment and/or housing, and sometimes result in the loss of custody of their children. According to the Center for Community Change, two-thirds of people detained in jails report an income of less than $12,000. We request a report within 90 days on the feasibility and next steps for City Council to take the following actions: 1. Unilaterally, automatically and annually purge and dismiss capiases and warrants that are seven years old for low-lying, non-violent misdemeanor crimes. (BALANCE ON FILE IN THE CLERK’S OFFICE) (STATEMENT ATTACHED).
sm: Requests feasibility report on automatically dismissing seven-year-old warrants for non-violent misdemeanors to help employment and housing access.

t: Reposition Center for Closing the Health Gap as operating budget line item
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, Councilmembers Johnson and Parks, WE MOVE that the City of Cincinnati reposition the Center for Closing the Health Gap as a line item in its operating budget - as it was historically - and remove it from the category of Human Services. The Center for Closing the Health Gap is not a human services provider. Rather, its mission is to eliminate racial and health disparities in the Greater Cincinnati community through education, advocacy, and outreach targeting the African American, Latino, and White Appalachian populations. The vision of Closing the Health Gap is to make Greater Cincinnati a healthier region for all. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Moves Center for Closing the Health Gap from Human Services category to operating budget line item.

sm: Requests administration report on Project Labor Agreement impacts including wages, costs, safety, and diversity within ninety days.

t: Charter amendment petition for Metropolitan Planning Organization membership requirements
rt: PETITION, submitted by the Clerk of Council, I hereby confirm that the Clerk’s office has received 579 petitions from J. P. Burleigh, on July 25, 2024, for an amendment to the Charter of the City of Cincinnati regarding Article XVII - Membership in a Metropolitan Planning Organization (“MPO”) (1) The City may commence or maintain membership in a MPO only when both of the following conditions are met: (a) a voting power of the governing board of the MPO is apportioned proportionally based on population, and (b) members that present local governments have at least 90% of the total votes on the governing board. (2) In the event that an MPO does not comply with section (1) of the Article, the City shall withdraw its membership from the body if the voting system is not corrected within 60 days of the effective date of this Article.
sm: Petition requiring Cincinnati's MPO membership only when voting power is proportionally apportioned by population.

t: Human Services Funding Priorities for Biennial Budget Cycles
rt: ORDINANCE (EMERGENCY), submitted by Councilmember Owens, from Emily Smart Woerner, City Solicitor, ESTABLISHING the City of Cincinnati’s human services funding priorities for the first year of the biennial budget, beginning with FY 2026, the second year of the biennial budget (budget update), beginning with FY 2025, and subsequent budgets and fiscal social innovation project to be awarded only in the first year of the biennial budget, and a revised multi-year funding cycle for all human services funding; ADVISING the United Way and any organization assisting the City with evaluating human services funding applications that Council’s priorities for the first year of the biennial budget, beginning with FY 2026, are to allocate up to 33 percent of appropriated human services funding for the Impact Award with any balance, if less than 33 percent is allocated to the large-scale social innovation project, allocated to organizations that further the work of the category selected for the Impact Award; 25 percent for Comprehensive Workforce Development Support; twenty percent for Youth Gun Violence Prevention and Reduction; ten percent for Supporting, Securing, and Stabilizing Housing for High-Risk Populations; ten percent for Emergency Wrap-Around Services through Project LIFT; and two percent for evaluating human services funding applications that Council’s priorities for the second year of biennial budget (budget update), beginning with FY 2025, are to allocate 33 percent of appropriated human services funding for organizations that further the work of the category selected for the Impact Award in the first year of the biennial budget; 25 percent for Comprehensive Workforce Development Support; twenty percent for Youth Gun Violence Prevention and Reduction; ten percent for Supporting, Securing and Stabilizing Housing for High-Risk Populations; ten percent for Emergency Wrap-Around Services through Project Lift; and two percent for overhead; and ADVSING the United Way and any organization assisting the City with evaluating human services funding applications that future Impact Awards categories will be determined by Council for the first year of each biennial budget.
sm: Establishes funding allocation percentages for human services programs including workforce development, violence prevention, and housing support.

t: Human Services Funding Priorities and Impact Award Program for FY 2026-2027
rt: ORDINANCE (EMERGENCY), submitted by Councilmember Owens, from Emily Smart Woerner, City Solicitor, ESTABLISHING the City’s human services funding priorities for the first year of the biennial budget, beginning with FY 2026, the second year of the biennial budget (budget update), beginning with FY 2027, and subsequent budgets and fiscal years; ESTABLISHING a human services funding Impact Award for one large-scale social innovation project to be awarded only in the first year of the biennial budget, and a revised multi-year funding cycle for all human services funding; ADVISING the United Way of Greater Cincinnati (“United Way”) and any organization assisting the City with evaluating human services funding applications that Council’s priorities for FY 2026 and FY 2027 are to allocate up to ten percent of appropriated human services funding for the Impact Award; 26 percent for Comprehensive Workforce Development Support; 26 percent for Youth Gun Violence Prevention and Reduction; 26 percent for Supporting, Securing, and Stabilizing Housing for High-Risk Populations; ten percent for Emergency Wrap-Around Services through Project LIFT; and two percent for overhead; ADVISING the United Way and any organization assisting the City with evaluating human services funding applications that applications that have previously applied directly to the City for Leveraged Support funding in the categories of Homelessness and Eviction Prevention, Human Services and Violence Prevention, or Workforce Programming and Poverty Reduction, should instead apply for human services funding; and ADVISING the United Way and any organization assisting the City with evaluating human services funding applications that future Impact Awards categories will be determined by Council for the first year of each biennial budget.
sm: Establishes funding priorities for human services including workforce development, gun violence prevention, housing stabilization, and creates Impact Award program.

t: Support for Ohio Parole Board reform and justice improvements
rt: RESOLUTION, from Paula Boggs Muething, City Solicitor, EXPRESSING the City of Cincinnati’s strong support for reform of the Ohio Parole Board; URGING that an independent investigation of policies, procedures, and practices of the Ohio Parole Board needs to be conducted; EXPRESSING support for an increase in the amount of time the Ohio Parole Board is given to review each case, resulting in greater concentration on the issues of each case and fewer distractions that could negatively impact the review process, EXPRESSING support for a revised attendance policy that decreases the number of hearings Ohio Parole Board members can miss and still be allowed to vote; OPPOSING the Ohio Parole Board’s current policy that ignores the need for interpreters for potential parolees whose first and primary language is not English; EXPRESSING support for a more diverse and inclusive Ohio Parole Board and Parole Board support staff; EXPRESSING support for a review of the practice of prosecutors in the hearings; URGING the Ohio General Assembly to separate the Parole Board from the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction; further ENCOURAGING the Ohio General Assembly and the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction to make the following changes to the Ohio Parole Board: that all votes of the Parole Board shall be made immediately following an institutional hearing and clemency hearing, and that such vote shall not be changed; that members of the public and the media shall not be removed from clemency death penalty or full board hearings unless requested by the offender or due to life-threatening situations; that Parole Board members shall elect a Chair for a term of two years and that Chair shall serve only one term as Chair during that six-year period; that Parole Board members shall not hold victim’s or offender’s conferences or be required to attend self-defense classes, which ignores the duties of their position; that the Parole Board shall cease to address or refer to offenders as “inmates” but shall address and refer to these individuals as “offenders”; and that eligible offenders may have their sentences converted from indefinite sentences to the minimum of their indefinite sentences if they meet reasonable suitability factors established by the General Assembly to achieve this purpose; and REAFFIRMING that the City of Cincinnati is a city that supports and encourages justice, fairness, and an end to mass incarceration.
sm: Expresses Cincinnati's support for comprehensive reforms to Ohio Parole Board policies, procedures, and independence.

t: Payment to Mercantile Library for Poet Laureate Program
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, WE MOVE that City Council pay to the Mercantile Library the sum of $10,000 from the City Managers General Fund as a moral obligation for the City of Cincinnati’s Poet Laureate Program. The City of Cincinnati established its Poet Laureate Program in 2016. The Mercantile Library agreed to manage the program in 2021 and has consistently done so. The budget for the Poet Laureate’s stipend is $10,000 per year. The Mercantile Library and City of Cincinnati each incur half of the $10,000 annual cost. The City of Cincinnati paid it’s $5,000 share to the Mercantile Library for the Cincinnati Poet Laureate Program in 2021, 2022, and 2023. However, the City of Cincinnati failed to pay to the Mercantile Library its $5,000 share for the Poet Laureate Program for FY’24 and owes for FY 25. Therefore, the total owed to the Mercantile Library for those two years is $10,000.
sm: Pays $10,000 to Mercantile Library for two years of overdue Poet Laureate Program costs.

t: Create Unity Fund for neighborhood events organized by community councils
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, WE MOVE that City Council create a Unity Fund for neighborhood events organized by community councils and/or other neighborhood groups. While the events may have another primary purpose, such events shall uplift the community, and strengthen bonds between neighbors. The City had a similar fund for community events several years ago. The Unity Fund will start with $100,000 in seed money from the FY’25 Carryover Budget.  WE MOVE further that the administration establish criteria and an application process for distribution of the Unity Fund, as well as an ongoing refunding strategy. (STATEMENT ATTACHED).
sm: Creates $100,000 Unity Fund to support neighborhood events that strengthen community bonds and uplift neighborhoods.

t: Allocate $69,000 for West End Sports Bar and Grill completion
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, WE MOVE that City Council allocate $69,000 from the Carryover Budget for ‘FY25 for completion of the West End Sports Bar and Grill, to be located at 1776 Linn Street in the West End neighborhood of Cincinnati. After years of planning, the West End Sports Bar and Grill has begun construction. The following items will allow this long-awaited project to cross the finish line: Installation of a fire alarm system that is more than Municipal Building Code requires in order to protect patrons and employees, as well as the city’s investment. Estimated cost: $25,000. Installation of a backflow air system in the kitchen to ameliorate extreme heat, especially in summer months. This feature was recommended by architects, Shawn Jacobs Engineering, and the installer, Viking HVAC. Estimated Cost $22,000. (BALANCE ON FILE IN CLERK’S OFFICE) (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Allocates $69,000 from carryover budget to complete West End Sports Bar and Grill construction project.

t: Allocate $350,000 to Habitat for Humanity for West End affordable housing properties
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, WE MOVE that City Council allocate to Habitat for Humanity $350,000 from the FY’25 Carryover Budget to help to meet Cincinnati’s urgent need for affordable housing, and affordable homeownership in particular. The funds will support the acquisition of nine (9) properties in the West End neighborhood of Cincinnati. After several months of negotiating, Habitat has gained temporary control of the sites. If Habitat is not funded, the properties will likely go to speculators. Habitat has completed four (4) homes on York Street in the West End which created a 200 percent increase in housing production north of Liberty Street for this census over the past 25 years. Habitat responsible for creating more than 700 new homes in Cincinnati.
sm: Allocates $350,000 from carryover budget to Habitat for Humanity to acquire nine West End properties for affordable housing.

t: Allocate $250,000 to Art Academy of Cincinnati for safety and infrastructure improvements
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, WE MOVE that City Council allocate to the Art Academy of Cincinnati $250,000 from the FY’25 Carryover Budget to support increased safety measures and infrastructure of the college. See Attachment A. The AAC is committed to community safety, accessibility, and the well-being of students in the five block radius immediately surrounding our AAC college in OTR. The college is situated at a busy intersection with high pedestrian traffic, and must prioritize safety and security, while also addressing broader community concerns and reducing local crime through proactive engagement. In addition to serving several hundred students, faculty, and staff, the AAC fosters an inclusive neighborhood by hosting events, public art projects, and collaborative initiatives that engage thousands of Cincinnati residents and tourists annually.
sm: Motion to allocate $250,000 from carryover budget to Art Academy for safety measures and infrastructure improvements.

t: Allocate $250,000 to Center for Closing the Health Gap
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Kearney, WE MOVE that City Council allocate to the Center for Closing the Health Gap $250,000 from the FY’25 Carryover Budget to support its impactful programming to empower residents in improving their health, and support the important work of tackling health disparities. Research shows that in Cincinnati, zip code determines lifespan (See Attachment.) The prevalence of cardiovascular disease and diabetes, and the increase of Type 2 diabetes in adults and children driven by lifestyle factors are central to the Center for Closing the Health Gap’s work. (BALANCE ON FILE IN THE CLERK’S OFFICE)
sm: Allocates $250,000 from carryover budget to support health programming addressing disparities and chronic diseases.

WE MOVE that the City Manager immediately commence the creation of an Office of Strategic Growth (OSG) inside the City Manager's office with shared jurisdiction over: WE FURTHER MOVE that the City Manager take the necessary steps within 90 days to launch the OSG within the current Operating Budget for fiscal year 2026; WE FURTHER MOVE that the City Administration prepare and provide a report within 90 days detailing the necessary additional staffing and budget requirements to fully empower the OSG to sustainably execute on its duties and responsibilities in pursuit of the City's strategic objectives and growth goals, so that such requirements can be taken into consideration by Council for updating the 2027 Operating Budget; WE FURTHER MOVE that the City Administration prepare and provide a report within 120 days with a plan and budget to complete a comprehensive strategic review of the City's development (BALANCE ON FILE IN CLERKS OFFICE) (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Establishes new Office of Strategic Growth to coordinate city development and growth initiatives.

t: Assessment of lighting and camera needs in city parks and recreational areas
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Albi and Jeffreys. WE MOVE that the Administration prepare a report within 30 days assessing the need for additional lighting and camera infrastructure across city parks, playgrounds and recreational areas owned by Cincinnati Parks and the Cincinnati Recreation Commission, with priority given to locations that have already experienced shootings and the five neighborhoods experiencing the highest levels of gun violence. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration prepare a separate subsequent report within 30 days of the initial report outlining the costs associated with installing, operating, and maintaining recommended lighting and camera improvements identified in the initial report, including any potential funding sources. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Administration to assess and report on lighting and camera infrastructure needs for city parks and recreational areas.

t: STATEMENT, submitted by Councilmember P.G. Sittenfeld, (Dissent) As a member of
rt: STATEMENT, submitted by Councilmember P.G. Sittenfeld, (Dissent) As a member of Council, in accordance with Rule 6.9, I express and present this official dissent from part of item #201701678 on the most recent Council meeting agenda, which occurred on December 20th, 2017. While the neighborhood project voted on in item #201701678 is both worth and exciting, included in that ordinance was an exemption to the application of the local Prevailing Wage Law. Prevailing Wages date back to the period following the Civil War; such legislation began to be passed at the state level in the late 19th-century; and Prevailing Wage was enshrined in Federal Law as part of the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931. Prevailing Wage legislation is vital for our economy and our workforce, helping to ensure quality, as well as to grant workers fair compensation for the dignity and value of their work. In no way should Council's recent individual instance of providing an exemption to Prevailing Wage-as requested by the Mayor and supported by a number of local building trade unions-be misconstrued as setting any future precedent, or undermining the City of Cincinnati's support for the application of Prevailing Wage. Further, as a Member of Council, I want to unequivocally affirm my support for Prevailing Wage as a key tool for providing pathways of opportunity for working families and our brothers and sisters in the building and construction trades.

rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Sittenfeld, WE MOVE that in 2017 Cincinnati City Council passed legislation and supported the City's Golden Cincinnati initiative, to further Cincinnati's desire to make Cincinnati an aging-friendly city; and WE MOVE that by 2030, one in every 5 Americans will be over the age of 65, and cities need to take steps to ensure preparedness for such shifting demographics; and WE MOVE that throughout the last year, the City has embraced the goals of becoming more livable for all residents, including those who are older and those who are differently abled, including hiring a Chief Advocacy Officer for Aging and Accessibility; and WE MOVE that to further the goals of the Golden Cincinnati Initiative, City Council desires the City Administration to join over 200 communities nationwide who make up the AARP Livable Communities network, which supports cities working to achieve goals like improved safety, pedestrian friendliness, age-friendly and accessible housing and transportation, access to medical care and social services for seniors, and otherwise providing opportunities for residents of all ages to actively participate in community life; and WE MOVE that participation in this network will unlock resources and grant opportunities, provide access to best practices and sharing of ideas among peer cities, create a proven framework for planning and community engagement, and put Cincinnati on the list of cities preparing for the future. NOW THEREFORE, we move that the City Administration, with the support of and at the direction of Council, undertake the steps to join the AARP Livable Communities network.
sm: Motion to join AARP network supporting aging-friendly and accessible communities.

t: Continental Crosswalk Standard Near Schools Parks
rt: MOTION, *(AMENDED) submitted by Councilmembers Seelbach, Dennard, Sittenfeld, Landsman, Young, Mann, Murray, Pastor and Vice Mayor Smitherman, WE MOVE that the Administration adopt the Continental Crosswalk as the standard crosswalk design for all marked crossings adjacent to any school, recreation center, playground, park facility, *shared use path or recreational trail. Within all Cincinnati Neighborhood Business Districts as defined by the Department of Community & Economic Development's Business District Boundary list. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration update these crosswalks to the improved standard as they are repainted as part of the needed maintenance and as streets are repaved as part of the CAP program or their regularly scheduled resurfacing. By upgrading the crosswalks as they are due for improvements, the costs of the safety upgrades are spread out within our already planned improvement projects. (STATEMENT ATTACHED) (AMENDED ON THE FLOOR OF COUNCIL 2/22/2018)
sm: Motion to adopt Continental Crosswalk design at schools and recreation areas.

t: Workplace Accommodations and Child-Friendly Meeting Policies
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Mann, Young, Dennard, Seelbach and Landsman, WE MOVE that the administration report on its compliance with section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act as amended by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (P.L. 111-148), which requires employers to designate a space other than a bathroom that is shielded from view and free from intrusion from coworkers and the public and may be used by an employee to express breast milk; WE FURTHER MOVE that the administration report on its existing policies and any improvements it can reasonably make upon them to ensure that public meetings are child-friendly, such as providing childcare for meetings where a large turnout is expected or setting aside a corner of the public meeting room and providing books and toys so they can quietly occupy themselves; WE FURTHER MOVE that the administration install diaper changing tables in the men's and women's restrooms on the third floor of City Hall. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Motion on breast milk expression space, childcare, and diaper changing facilities.

Hours of training Metro bus drivers receive annually 4. Average number of miles that Metro buses are driven each year 5. Average number of accidents Metro buses are involved in each year that result in (1) property damage, and (2) personal injury 6. Top reasons for bus accidents 7. For Metro bus drivers employed by Metro as of January 1, 2018, how many bus drivers have been involved in (1) 1-10 accidents, (2) 11-20 of accidents, (3) 21-30 accidents, and (4) 31 or more? 8. Metro policy for bus drivers who are involved in a preventable or at-fault for an accident (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Request report on Metro bus driver accidents and training data

t: Smart City Technology Advisory Council Creation
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Sittenfeld, Landsman, Mann, Dennard, Seelbach, Pastor, Murray, Young and Vice Smitherman, WE MOVE that the City of Cincinnati is moving forward with investments in making Cincinnati a Smart City, investing in and planning for technology changes and upgrades; WE MOVE that our community is full of highly-talented technologists whose expertise could be tapped to benefit the decision-making, service delivery, and problem-solving of local government. WE MOVE that the City Administration prepare a report on the creation and activation of a Government Technology Advisory Council for the benefit of the City; WE MOVE that such a board be voluntary and unpaid, with between 5 and 7 members appointed by the Mayor and confirmed by City Council, holding not less than two regular standing meetings per year in addition to ad hoc meetings to trouble-shoot timely City technology issues; WE MOVE that such a board report to and be staffed by the Officer of the City Manager.
sm: Move to create Government Technology Advisory Council for smart city investments and technology decisions.

t: Job Creation Tax Credit Minimum Qualifying Wage Implementation
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Seelbach, Dennard, Mann, Sittenfeld, Young and Landsman, WE MOVE that the Administration adopt and implement the following Minimum Qualifying Wage when offering Job Creation Tax Credits: July 1, 2018 - For any new JCTC proposal the employer must have a $12.30 minimum wage for all jobs eligible under the tax credit. Jan 1, 2019 - For any new JCTC proposal the employer must have a $13.50 minimum wage for all jobs eligible under the tax credit. July 1, 2019 - For any new JCTC proposal the employer must have a $15 minimum wage for all jobs eligible under the tax credit. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration define qualifications for a Workforce Training JCTC which would be eligible to lower wage positions where the intent is boosting opportunity for hard-to-place employees and individuals with barriers to employment. Additionally, the Administration is requested to provide an FYI on the MQ and its relation to new JCTC's biannually for the next 2 years beginning in late 2018. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Implement tiered minimum wage requirements for new JCTC proposals and create workforce training eligibility provisions.

t: Chapter 318 and 320 Amendment Motion
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Young, Sittenfeld, Landsman, Dennard and Seelbach, WE MOVE that the Administration draft an ordinance to make the following amendments to Chapter 318 and 320 of the Cincinnati Municipal Code: 1) Amend Chapter 320 to recognize the updated MBE/WBE inclusion categories adopted by Council in 2015, allowing these to match with waivers and contract exemptions of SBE program participants within Chapter 320. This ensures smaller, minority businesses continue to participate as is (and can continue to grow). 2. Amend Chapter 320 to clarify that project-specific partnerships between a Bidder/Contractor and an Apprenticeship Program for the Primary Apprenticeable Occupation qualifies the bid. This ensures any bidders can be the prime contractor by partnering with a qualified apprenticeship. 3) Amend Chapter 320-3 to clarify that the 10-day response period includes proof of qualifying for the Apprenticeship Requirements listed in 320-5. This ensures an efficient bidding process allowing all bidders to comply. 4) Amend Chapter 320 to remove language referring to the now defunct Department of Sewers, placing administration of Chapter 320 under the Department of Economic Inclusion. 5) Review, for a period of no more than 6-months, Chapter 318 to correct significant flaws, which currently incentivize the hiring of Kentucky & Indiana workers while disincentivizing the hiring of Cincinnati & Hamilton County workers. If the Administration prefers, include in the ordinance a suspension of Chapter 318 to allow time to correct these flaws and ensure local laws support not undermine the hiring of local workers and contracting with minority & women owned firms. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Motion to amend local hiring and MBE/WBE contracting requirements chapters.

t: Streetcar Management and Oversight

The analysis should specifically examine the roles of the City, SORTA and Transdev and provide a recommendation to Council on best way forward for its management structure and operations. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)

t: Children and Families Budget and Council Establishment
rt: MOTION (AMENDED), submitted by Councilmembers Landsman, Dennard, Young, Sittenfeld, Seelbach and Pastor, Cincinnati has one of the highest rates of poverty in the country, and far too many of our children and families are suffering. Many cities have taken significant steps to better support children and families, through strategic partnerships, investments, and leadership (usually by way of an Office for Children and Families). To take meaningful steps toward real action on behalf of our children and families, WE MOVE that the Administration establish for Council and the Mayor a "Children and Families" Budget detailing our current investments in city-funded programs and projects that directly or indirectly support children and or families. This should be done as part of the budget process so that we, and the community, can better understand where we are investing now and where we are now. To further clarify, we simply want to pull out from the city's budget, in a separate document, those items that represent our current investments on behalf of children and families to better understand where we currently support children and families and where we might need to offer additional support. This is all done as part of a larger effort to do more to help make Cincinnati a better place for our children and families. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration identify a point person to work with the Council on the formation of a Children and Families Council, detailed in the attached overview of such a council.
sm: Motion to establish separate children and families budget and council to better track investments.

t: Designation Wage Monitor Living Wage Advisory Committee
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Landsman, Dennard, Young, Sittenfeld and Seelbach, Cincinnati has passed several wage-related ordinances that are aimed to protect workers and lift wages. To help assist in this effort. WE MOVE that the Administration designate a Wage Monitor to further ensure our wage-related ordinances are being adhered to throughout our city. Once the city's Wage Monitor is identified, WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration hold a press conference with key stakeholders and disseminate the pertinent information to all relevant parties.  It will be important for the community to know who the Wage Monitor is, and how to reach them. WE FURTHER MOVE the Administration to consider a 1-800 phone number to make it as easy as possible for workers and others to reach someone to help. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration ask that this new Wage Monitor convene a Living Wage Advisory Committee of employers and labor representatives to recommend further steps to protect workers and improve wages.
sm: Motion to designate wage monitor and establish living wage advisory committee to enforce wage ordinances.

t: Install stop signs Kroger and Overland
rt: MOTION, (AMENDED) submitted by Councilmembers Sittenfeld, Dennard, Pastor, Seelbach, Mann, and Landsman, Whereas, Cincinnati City Council is committed to pedestrian safety and supports Neighborhoods that are taking action to address issues of speeding and safety on their streets and Whereas, the residents of Kroger Avenue have undertaken all reasonable steps to mitigate speeding and pedestrian safety on their street, working with DOTE, and that it has been determined that no engineering fixes are workable on a street with the grade, sightlines and location of Kroger; and Whereas the residents have circulated a petition that shows their desire to address the issue of speeding and pedestrian safety on Kroger; and Whereas, the residents desire stop signs to be placed at the corner of Kroger and Overland, and the Mt. Lookout Community Council has submitted a letter of support for such stop signs, citing, among other things, several near misses and the failure of previous street calming measures; and Whereas, Cincinnati City Council expressly supports the idea of stop signs being used for speed control on particularly dangerous streets where no other solutions are viable; and Therefore, WE MOVE that the Department of Traffic and Engineering work to install stop signs at the intersection of Kroger and Overland. *Well lit crosswalks at that intersection.
sm: Install stop signs at Kroger and Overland intersection for pedestrian safety.

t: Council Rules amendment staff meetings appointments
rt: MOTION, dated 05/11/2018, submitted by Councilmember Landsman, WE MOVE that the* following provisions in the Rules of Council are amended as follows: Rule 1.7. Weekly staff meetings. In order to promote a collegial and collaborative working environment, the offices shall agree upon a weekly standing meeting among the Members' and Mayor's Chiefs of Staff. 3.5 Appointment by the Mayor. Within the first 30 days of the Term, the Clerk of Council shall provide the Members with a list of those positions appointed by the Mayor with the advice and consent of Council which will expire during the Term. When the Mayor submits a proposed appointment to Members, the name of the proposed appointee shall he published in the City Bulletin and consideration of the appointment shall be at the next regular meeting of Council. Any Member may request an additional week for consideration of the appointment, but requests from all Members may not aggregate to extend the additional consideration period for more than one week. t: Adopt 2018 Green Cincinnati Plan with exceptions
rt: MOTION, dated 5/16/2018, submitted by Mayor John Cranley, WE MOVE that the City of Cincinnati adopt the 2018 Green Cincinnati Plan with the following exceptions: 1. Remove the recommendation to require all tenant-occupied rental residences to have at least one air-conditioned room. Landlords can and will pass the costs to their renters, posing additional financial burdens to tenants - especially those in disadvantaged neighborhoods.  Furthermore, air conditioning poses negative effects on the environment.  Imposing this fee unilaterally will increase our carbon footprint by amplifying electricity consumption and carbon emissions. 2. Remove the recommendation to implement a fee or ban to discourage use of single-use bags. Rather, we should work collaboratively with grocers and other retail outlets to find a positive solution that reduces waste without imposing a financial burden on Cincinnati families. Imposing this fee would create a regressive tax for consumers and will disproportionately affect working and low-income families, fixed-income seniors, and individuals without vehicles. In addition, taking money out of the pockets of consumers mean some people have less money for food. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Motion to adopt Green Cincinnati Plan excluding air conditioning requirement and single-use bag fee recommendations.

t: Strong Cincinnati Partnership with Mayerson Academy
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Landsman, Dennard, Seelbach, Sittenfeld, Young, Murray and Pastor, WE MOVE that the Administration form a "Strong Cincinnati" partnership with Mayerson Academy, with the support from the Mayerson Foundation, whose mission is to activate the strengths within individuals, organizations and neighorhoods, to help to improve the way in which City Hall works and strengthen the culture within our city whereby people are more likely to be working together, across race and income for the betterment of their communities. WE FURTHER MOVE that everyone at City Hall take the VIA Survey, a strengths-based survey that focuses on one's best qualities and for Mayerson Academy, the exclusive education partner to the VIA Institute, the global leader in character science, to provide the appropriate training and support to City Hall and department officials and staff ( the equivalent of 4 full days and a total of three additional coaching days, which will require 2 release days for staff participants), beginning with elected officials, department heads and other members of senior administration. The administration of the survey and training will be privately funded. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration will work with the Mayerson Foundation and Mayerson Academy to establish and manage a Strong Cincinnati Working Group made up of people from across the City who want to work on what would be a cultural, strengths-based shift within and outside of City Hall. The Working Group would make ongoing recommendations and provide guidance and support for engaging neighborhoods in scaling the work across the city.
sm: Motion to form Strong Cincinnati partnership for cultural and organizational strengthening.

t: Property and Earnings Tax Relief for Childcare Providers
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmembers Landsman, Dennard, Seelbach, Sittenfeld and Young, Most community-based childcare and preschool providers struggle with the resources necessary to achieve and sustain quality, which is critical the children they serve, and the city  can play a meaningful role in providing much needed assistance in this regard. Therefore; WE MOVE that the Administration prepare a report on the feasibility of providing property and earnings tax relief to community-based childcare and preschool providers, both center-based and home-based. Relief should come in the form of incentives for these providers to pursue, achieve and maintain quality ratings. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration work with the necessary partners, including the Cincinnati Preschool Promise, the Community Action Agency and 4C for Children to determine how best to provide such tax relief.
sm: Motion to explore tax relief for community-based childcare and preschool providers.

t: Rules of Council Comprehensive Amendments
rt: MOTION, (AMENDED) submitted by Councilmember Landsman, WE MOVE that the following provisions in the Rules of Council are amended as follows: Rule 1.7. Weekly staff meetings, In order to promote a more collegial and collaborative working environment, the offices are encouraged to agree upon regular, voluntary meetings among the Members' and Mayor's Chiefs of Staff. 3.5 Appointment by the Mayor. Within the first 30 days of the Term, the Clerk of Council shall provide the Members with a list of those positions appointed by the Mayor with the advice and consent of Council which will expire during the Term. When the Mayor submits a proposed appointment to Members, the name of the proposed appointee shall be published in the City Bulletin and consideration of the appointment shall be at the next meeting of Council. Any Members may request an additional week for consideration of the appointment, but requests from all Members may not aggregate to extend the additional consideration period for more than one week. A majority of Members may reject any request for an additional week. 7.9 Council Referrals. Items on the calendar, which have not been previously referred to Committee, shall be referred to the appropriate Committee by the Mayor within two weeks of appearing on the Council Calendar. Items shall be referred to the planning commission where required by the Charter or law. Planning commission items shall be initially referred to the commission and to the appropriate Committee. When returned to Council by the planning commission, the items shall be placed on the Committee agenda with the initial referral. A non-legislative item may be considered immediately without referral to Committee, and then acted upon only upon an affirmative vote of two-thirds of the Members. 10.2 Standing Committees. (a) The Standing Committees of Council, commencing January 2, 2018 shall be: (1) Budget and Finance Committee; (2) Economic Growth and Zoning Committee; (3) Education, Innovation and Growth Committee; (4) Equity, Inclusion, Youth and The Arts Committee; (5) Law and Public Safety Committee; (6) Major Projects and Smart Government Committee; (7) Neighborhood Committee. 10.8 Committee Reports. A report in its final form, if approved by the Committee which caused the report to be created, action on the report in the form of a resolution or ordinance shall be sent to the Mayor's office to be placed on the council calendar in a timely fashion. Any item that was reviewed and considered in Committee on which there was a tie vote; no action; or other failure to pass out of Committee may be referred by any Member of the Committee to the Mayor for consideration by the Mayor as to whether the item should be placed on the agenda of Council. In addition, any legislation properly referred will get a vote in the full Council by a request of any Member of Council or the Mayor. The Clerk of Council shall transmit to Council in writing the reports of Committees containing the recommended disposition of matters referred to them. Written indication on the calendars as to a Committee recommendation shall satisfy the requirement that reports of Committees be transmitted in writing to Council. *(AMENDED ON FLOOR OF COUNCIL)
sm: Amended motion to revise multiple Rules of Council sections for operational efficiency.

t: Free Streetcar Ridership Initiative and Parking Trust
rt: MOTION, submitted by Councilmember Mann, WE MOVE that the City pursue the goal of eliminating charges for Streetcar ridership. WE FURTHER MOVE that, as a first step, commercial and residential parking requirements in the Downtown and Over-the-Rhine (OTR) neighborhoods be waived for any developer who contributes 40% of what would have been its required parking investment into a "Parking Trust Fund." WE FURTHER MOVE that the Parking Trust Fund be used to reduce or eliminate all fares to ride the streetcar. (STATEMENT ATTACHED)
sm: Motion to eliminate streetcar fares via parking requirement waivers and trust fund.

t: Streetcar Management and Operations Improvements
rt: MOTION, dated 05/21/2018, submitted by Councilmembers Landsman, Seelbach, Young, After several months of fact finding, and a commitment to doing what is best for riders and taxpayers, WE MOVE the Administration adopt the following "fixes" to the Streetcar: 1.	 Using existing resources, establish a new position of Executive Director of the Streetcar, reporting into both City Hall and SORTA (see proposed updated management chart attached), and working with support from a reinvigorated Streetcar nonprofit organization (NPO) with corporate and community leaders. The Executive Director must be empowered to manage all aspects of the Streetcar Operations, including all contracts and decisions. With contracts and decisions split between City Hall and SORTA, this new leader is arguably the only way to establish an effective management structure in the short-run. This structure begins to mirror the successful streetcar project in Kansas City. The Administration should continue to look at all long-term management options per Councilwoman Murray's request. 2. Until a new Streetcar Executive Director has been hired, provide to Council and the Mayor: 1. Performance and financial reviews and reports on the Transdev and CAF contracts. 2. A set of new performance measures for Streetcar excellence, with regular reporting. 3. An expedited plan to repair the vehicles, with details on what needs fixed and by when it will be fixed. 4. A plan to resolve blockage issues, particularly as they relate to enforcement and with buses at and around Government Square (as well as other identified "problem spots" along the route, and to shorten headways within the context of the traffic study. 5. A report on the feasibility (and what would be required) to make the Streetcar free in a way that would increase ridership (and in a budget neutral way). 6. New PR, marketing, and advertising plans within thirty days that are well designed and proactive and the development of a working group focused on these activities. 7. A report on the financial impact on expanding the VTICA program, and the feasibility of an OTR/CBD special assessment. 8. A recommended proposal for appointing members to the reinvigorated nonprofit, and its initial purpose. We would ask that the new Executive Director would continue to pursue these requests. 3. Establish a cross-sector working group to address short- and long-term budget issues. WE FURTHER MOVE that the Administration work with SORTA to bring back a proposal within two weeks that address these recommendations.
sm: Establish Executive Director position for Streetcar; address management, performance, and financial issues.

t: Tree removal management and safety action plan
rt: MOTION, submitted by Vice Mayor Smitherman, Councilmembers Young, Landsman, Pastor, Dennard and Mann, WE MOVE that the City Administration provide a comprehensive report to Cincinnati City Council on the number of trees throughout the city that have been marked or removal and any trees on the preventative maintenance list. (BACKGROUND) On April 19, 2015 65 year-old Cincinnati retired music teacher Jacqueline Carr was driving home and was near Berkley and Reading Road just a few blocks from her street Avonlea in Bond Hill when a tree that was marked for removal for 11 months by the Cincinnati Parks Department fell on her vehicle and killed Ms. Carr.
